---
title: "The cost of blocking a good email"
subtitle: "A reproducible Julia publishing pilot"
engine: julia
---

A classifier can have impressive accuracy and still make expensive mistakes.
Blocking an invoice may cost more than letting an advertisement reach an inbox.
This experiment uses the same simulation and evaluation functions as chapter 14.
Changing the source code changes both the chapter's examples and this report.

This is synthetic email data, not an estimate of the performance of a deployed
spam filter. Each email has one of four pre-delivery signals and a binary label.
We use separate training, validation, and test rows. We choose a decision rule on
validation data and inspect its test performance once after that choice.

## Fit the scores

```{julia}
include(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "..", "14_model_evaluation", "core.jl"))
using .ModelEvaluation
mail = synthetic_mail()
rows = split_rows(length(mail.label))
score = fit_score(mail.signal[rows.train], mail.label[rows.train])
validation_probability = predict_score(score, mail.signal[rows.validation])
```

The scores estimate how often each signal is associated with spam. A score is
not a decision: we still have to choose when to block an email. If probabilities
are calibrated for the population in which the filter is used, and correct
classifications have zero cost, the expected costs of the two actions are

$$L(\mathrm{block}) = C_{FP}(1-p), \qquad L(\mathrm{allow}) = C_{FN}p.$$

Blocking minimizes expected cost when $p \geq C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})$.
This formula depends on calibration and the stated costs. It does not guarantee
that the scores above are calibrated. Here we instead compare candidate
thresholds by their observed validation cost.

## Choose the operating point

Set the cost of blocking legitimate mail to five units and missing spam to one.
These are illustrative preferences, not universal business values.

```{julia}
false_positive_cost = 5.0
false_negative_cost = 1.0
choice = choose_threshold(mail.label[rows.validation], validation_probability;
    false_positive_cost, false_negative_cost)
choice
```

Only now do we score the held-out test set. The comparison with an always-allow
baseline is especially useful when spam is uncommon. We report both accuracy
and cost because they answer different questions.

```{julia}
test_probability = predict_score(score, mail.signal[rows.test])
test_labels = mail.label[rows.test]
selected = confusion(test_labels, test_probability; threshold=choice.threshold)
baseline = confusion(test_labels, zeros(length(test_labels)); threshold=0.5)
(; selected=(metrics=metrics(selected),
             cost=mean_cost(selected; false_positive_cost, false_negative_cost)),
   always_allow=(metrics=metrics(baseline),
                 cost=mean_cost(baseline; false_positive_cost, false_negative_cost)))
```

A single held-out result is still uncertain. For a real system, collect more
representative data, assess variability, and monitor whether the population or
costs change. Do not repeatedly adjust the rule after inspecting this test set
and continue calling it held out.

## Explore without reusing the test set

The chapter 14 Pluto notebook lets you vary mistake costs and deployment
prevalence using validation data. Its prevalence experiment explicitly assumes
that class-conditional error rates stay fixed. That assumption can fail if spam
content changes; the slider is a thought experiment, not a deployment guarantee.

This pilot tests Quarto's native Julia engine while the existing book remains
in Bookdown. Render it from the repository root with
`quarto render publishing/quarto`. Quarto executes the code and produces a
standalone HTML report in `publishing/quarto/_site/decision-costs.html`.
